stem:
A student investigates how the horizontal range of a ball depends on the height from which it is launched. A spring launcher is clamped horizontally to a tall stand and fires a small steel ball, which lands on carbon paper on the floor.

The student measures the height $h$ of the launch point above the floor and the range $R$ from the point directly below the launch point (found with a plumb line) to each mark. The ball is fired five times at each height. The table gives the mean range and its uncertainty (half the range of the five readings), and $R^2$. The five readings for $h = 0.700\ \text{m}$ are given separately.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Identify one variable that the student must control so that the launch speed is the same for every shot.
markscheme: Any one of: how far the spring is compressed / the same ball / the launcher kept horizontal ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the mean range for $h = 0.700\ \text{m}$.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the absolute uncertainty in this mean range.
markscheme: Half the range of the readings: $\dfrac{0.925 - 0.909}{2} = 0.0080\ \text{m}$ (accept 0.0080 m or 0.00800 m) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Show that, if air resistance is negligible, $R^2 = \dfrac{2u^2}{g}h$, where $u$ is the launch speed.
markscheme: Vertical motion: $h = \tfrac12 g t^2$, so $t = \sqrt{\dfrac{2h}{g}}$ ✓
Horizontal motion at constant speed: $R = ut$, so $R^2 = u^2 \times \dfrac{2h}{g}$ ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Determine the gradient of the graph of $R^2$ against $h$.
markscheme: Draws a line of best fit and uses two well-separated points on it ✓
Gradient $= 1.20\ \text{m}$ (accept 1.15 to 1.26) ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: Determine the launch speed $u$.

mistakes.feedback: Check the factor of 2: the gradient is $2u^2/g$.
That is $u^2$: take the square root.

markscheme: Gradient $= \dfrac{2u^2}{g}$, so $u = \sqrt{\dfrac{g \times \text{gradient}}{2}}$ ✓
$u = 2.42\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (accept 2.37 to 2.48; allow ECF from (e)) ✓

parts.label: g
parts.question: The manufacturer states that the launch speed is $2.60\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Discuss whether the data support this statement.
markscheme: Uses the steepest and shallowest lines through the error bars (their own lines, or the uncertainty in the gradient) to find a range for $u$: the lines shown give about 2.38 to 2.48 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
2.60 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ is above this range, so the data do not support the statement (the launcher is slower than stated). Award this mark for a conclusion consistent with the candidate's own range ✓

stem:
A student releases a trolley from rest at a mark on a ramp. The trolley runs down the ramp onto a level runway, where it moves through a light gate. A card of length $L = (10.0 \pm 0.1)\ \text{cm}$ fixed to the trolley blocks the light beam, and a timer records the time $t$ for which the beam is blocked.

The student repeats the run seven times. The results are shown in the table.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Identify the trial that should not be used in the analysis. Justify your answer using the data.
markscheme: Trial 5 ($t = 0.180\ \text{s}$) ✓
It is about 0.025 s shorter than the mean of the other trials, much more than their spread (they lie within about $\pm 0.002\ \text{s}$ of each other) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Suggest one cause of this reading that is consistent with its value.
markscheme: The time is too short, so the trolley was moving faster than in the other runs: for example it was released from above the mark, or it was pushed as it was released ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the mean time $\bar{t}$ of the remaining trials.

parts.label: d
parts.question: Determine the absolute uncertainty in $\bar{t}$, using the spread of the remaining readings.
markscheme: Half the range of the remaining readings: $\pm 0.0020\ \text{s}$ (accept 0.002 s) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Determine the speed $v$ of the trolley as it passes through the light gate.

mistakes.feedback: Convert the card length to metres before dividing.

markscheme: $v = \dfrac{L}{\bar{t}}$ with $L$ in metres ✓
$v = 0.489\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (allow ECF from (c)) ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: State and explain the effect on the value of $v$ if trial 5 had been included.
markscheme: The mean time would be smaller, so $v$ would be larger (by about 2 %) and would not represent a release from the mark ✓

stem:
A student investigates how the extension $x$ of a spring depends on the load $F$ on it. The spring hangs from a clamp beside a vertical metre rule. Slotted masses are added to a hanger attached to the spring.

The student measures the extension from the position of the end of the spring with nothing attached. The student records as $F$ the weight of the slotted masses only.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Hooke's law suggests that $x$ is proportional to $F$. Explain how the graph shows that the student's values of $x$ are not proportional to $F$.
markscheme: The points lie on a straight line (each extension is uncertain by only ±1 mm) ✓
The line does not pass through the origin: it meets the extension axis (at $F = 0$) at about 19 mm, far more than the ±1 mm uncertainty ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the spring constant $k$ of the spring.
markscheme: Gradient $= \dfrac{1}{k}$: about 40.3 $\text{mm N}^{-1}$, converted to $\text{m N}^{-1}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Explain how leaving out the weight of the hanger accounts for the shape of the graph.
markscheme: The hanger's weight stretches the spring even when the recorded load is zero, so every extension is larger by the same amount ✓
The line is shifted up by a constant amount ($m_h g/k$) but its gradient is unchanged ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Use the graph to determine the mass $m_h$ of the hanger.
markscheme: The intercept on the extension axis (at $F = 0$) is the extension caused by the hanger alone: about 19 mm $= \dfrac{m_h g}{k}$ ✓
$m_h = 0.047\ \text{kg}$ (accept 0.041 to 0.054; allow ECF from (b)) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Another student calculates $k$ as $\dfrac{F}{x}$ using only the last row of the table. Calculate this value, and explain why it differs from your answer to (b).
markscheme: It is too small: $x$ includes the extension caused by the hanger but $F$ does not include its weight. The gradient method is not affected by a constant offset ✓

stem: A student investigates how the extension $x$ of a long, thin copper wire depends on the load $F$ on it. The wire hangs from a beam beside a second, identical reference wire, which carries a constant small load. Masses are added to the test wire, and a vernier scale fixed between the two wires measures the extension of the test wire.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Hooke's law predicts that $x$ is proportional to $F$. Use the graph to identify the range of loads for which the data are consistent with Hooke's law. Justify your answer.
markscheme: A straight line through the origin fits the points, within their uncertainty of ±0.05 mm, up to about 49.0 N (accept up to 58.8 N) ✓
For larger loads the points lie above any such line by far more than their uncertainty ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine $k$, the load per unit extension, in the region where Hooke's law holds.
markscheme: Gradient of the straight part of the graph $= \dfrac{1}{k}$, converted to $\text{m N}^{-1}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the extension that Hooke's law predicts for a load of 78.4 N, using your value of $k$. Compare it with the measured extension.
markscheme: $x = \dfrac{F}{k} = 8.28\ \text{mm}$ (allow ECF from (b)) ✓
The measured value, 9.15 mm, is about 0.87 mm larger, far more than its uncertainty of $\pm 0.05\ \text{mm}$: the wire stretches more than Hooke's law predicts ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Another student draws one line of best fit through all nine points and calculates $k$ from its gradient. Explain whether this value of $k$ would be larger or smaller than your answer to (b).
markscheme: The points beyond about 49.0 N lie above the straight line, so a line through all the points has a larger gradient (more extension per newton) ✓
Since $k = \dfrac{1}{\text{gradient}}$, this $k$ would be smaller (about 8200 $\text{N m}^{-1}$) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Suggest why the extension is measured relative to a reference wire hanging from the same beam.
markscheme: Changes in room temperature (thermal expansion) and any sagging of the beam affect both wires equally, so they do not change the measured extension ✓

stem:
A student stands still on a force plate, bends their knees, and then jumps straight up. The force plate records the vertical force $F$ on it 200 times per second. The student lands back on the plate with bent knees.

The graph shows the force recorded by the plate.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Explain why the force recorded in the first 0.10 s is equal to the student's weight.
markscheme: The student is at rest, so the resultant force is zero: the upward force from the plate equals the weight (and the student pushes down on the plate with an equal force) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the mass of the student.
markscheme: $F \approx 606\ \text{N}$, so $m = \dfrac{F}{g} = 62\ \text{kg}$ (accept 60 to 64 kg) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: The push starts at $t = 0.10\ \text{s}$. Estimate the impulse of the resultant force on the student from then until the student leaves the plate.
markscheme: Resultant force $= F - mg$: uses the area between the graph and a horizontal line at the weight ✓
Up to take-off at $t = 0.50\ \text{s}$ (where $F$ reaches zero); the area below the weight line near take-off is subtracted ✓
Impulse $\approx 150\ \text{N s}$ (accept 140 to 160 N s) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Determine the speed of the student at take-off.
markscheme: Impulse = change of momentum, from rest: $v = \dfrac{\text{impulse}}{m}$ ✓
$v = 2.4\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (accept 2.3 to 2.6; allow ECF from (b) and (c)) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The take-off speed can also be found from the time the student spends in the air, using $v = \dfrac{gt}{2}$. Determine this speed and compare it with your answer to (d).
markscheme: Time in the air from the graph: $1.06 - 0.50 = 0.56\ \text{s}$, so $v = 2.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ ✓
This is larger than the value from the impulse, by about 13 % (accept a comparison consistent with the candidate's values) ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: Suggest one reason why the speed from the time in the air is larger.
markscheme: The student lands with bent knees, so the centre of mass is lower at landing than at take-off: the student is in the air for longer than the rise and fall to the same height takes ✓

stem:
A student investigates how much energy a tennis ball keeps each time it bounces. The ball is released from rest and bounces several times on a hard floor. A phone films it at 30 frames per second in front of a height scale fixed to the wall.

For each bounce, the student finds the frame in which the ball is highest and reads the peak height $h$ of the bottom of the ball. The table and graph show the results. The point for bounce 4 has not been plotted.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Describe the energy transfers from the moment the ball is released until it reaches its highest point after the first bounce.
markscheme: Gravitational potential energy → kinetic energy as it falls; at the impact some energy is transferred to internal (thermal) energy and sound (the rest is stored elastically and returned as kinetic energy); kinetic → gravitational potential energy as it rises, so there is less at the top than at the start ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the ratio $\dfrac{h_1}{h_0}$ for the first bounce and the ratio $\dfrac{h_6}{h_5}$ for the last bounce.

parts.label: c
parts.question: Plot the point for bounce 4 on the graph.
markscheme: Point plotted at $n = 4$, $h = 18.5\ \text{cm}$, to within half a small square ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: The fraction of its energy that the ball keeps in a bounce is equal to $\dfrac{h_{n+1}}{h_n}$. Deduce, using the uncertainties in the heights, whether the data support the idea that every bounce keeps the same fraction of the energy.
markscheme: The fractional uncertainties of the two heights add: $\Delta\!\left(\dfrac{h_1}{h_0}\right) = 0.5525 \times \left(\dfrac{1.0}{200.0} + \dfrac{1.0}{110.5}\right)$, so $\dfrac{h_1}{h_0} = 0.553 \pm 0.008$ ✓

$\Delta\!\left(\dfrac{h_6}{h_5}\right) = 0.65 \times \left(\dfrac{1.0}{6.5} + \dfrac{1.0}{10.0}\right)$, so $\dfrac{h_6}{h_5} = 0.65 \pm 0.17$ (accept $0.7 \pm 0.2$): the small heights at the end have large fractional uncertainties ✓

A single value (about 0.55) lies within the uncertainty range of every ratio, so the data are consistent with a constant fraction; but the later ratios are imprecise, so they test the idea only weakly (award for a conclusion consistent with the candidate's ratios) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Predict the peak height after bounce 7.
markscheme: $h_7 \approx h_6 \times 0.55 = 3.6\ \text{cm}$, using the common ratio from (d) (or the mean ratio, or $h_0$ multiplied by the ratio 7 times; accept 3.0 to 4.1 cm) ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: Suggest one limitation of measuring the peak heights from this video, and its effect on the readings.
markscheme: Any one of: the frame nearest the top may not show the ball at its highest point, so the reading is slightly too low / the ball is nearer the camera than the scale (parallax), so its height read against the scale depends on where the camera is / the moving ball is blurred, so its bottom edge is hard to judge ✓

stem:
A student determines the specific heat capacity $c$ of aluminium. An electric heater is placed in a hole in an aluminium block of mass $m = (1.000 \pm 0.001)\ \text{kg}$. A thermometer in a second hole, filled with oil, measures the temperature $\theta$ of the block. The block is wrapped in insulation.

The heater is connected to a supply. The p.d. across it is $V = (12.0 \pm 0.1)\ \text{V}$ and the current in it is $I = (4.20 \pm 0.05)\ \text{A}$; both stay constant. The heater is switched on at $t = 0$. The table shows the temperature at different times. Each time is measured with an uncertainty of $\pm 1\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Determine the temperature change $\Delta T$ of the block during the 600 s of heating.

parts.label: b
parts.question: State the absolute uncertainty in $\Delta T$.
markscheme: Each temperature reading is uncertain by $\pm 0.5\ {}^{\circ}\text{C}$; for a difference the absolute uncertainties add, so $\Delta T$ is uncertain by $\pm 1.0\ {}^{\circ}\text{C}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium from these data.
markscheme: Energy supplied $E = VIt = 12.0 \times 4.20 \times 600 = 30240\ \text{J}$ ✓
$c = \dfrac{E}{m\Delta T} = 903\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ (allow ECF from (a)) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Identify, by comparing percentage uncertainties, the measured quantity that contributes most to the uncertainty in $c$.
markscheme: Percentage uncertainties: $V$: 0.83 %; $I$: 1.2 %; $t$: 0.2 %; $m$: 0.1 %; $\Delta T$: 3.0 % (at least three correct) ✓
$\Delta T$ contributes most ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Determine the absolute uncertainty in $c$. Hence state $c$ with its uncertainty, to an appropriate number of significant figures.
markscheme: Adds the percentage uncertainties: 5.3 %, so $\Delta c = 48\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ (allow ECF) ✓
$c = (900 \pm 50)\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$: uncertainty to 1 significant figure and $c$ rounded to the same place ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: Suggest one change to the method that would reduce the percentage uncertainty in $\Delta T$.
markscheme: Any one of: heat for longer (or use a more powerful heater) so that $\Delta T$ is larger / use a thermometer with a smaller division (for example a digital thermometer reading to $0.1\ {}^{\circ}\text{C}$) ✓

stem: A student determines the specific heat capacity $c$ of water. An electric immersion heater is placed in $(0.400 \pm 0.001)\ \text{kg}$ of water in a glass beaker with no lid and no insulation. The p.d. across the heater is $V = (12.0 \pm 0.1)\ \text{V}$ and the current in it is $I = (3.50 \pm 0.05)\ \text{A}$; both stay constant. The heater is switched on at $t = 0$ and the stirred water's temperature $\theta$ is recorded. Times are measured to $\pm 1\ \text{s}$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Use the data to show that the rate at which the temperature of the water rises decreases during the heating.
markscheme: In the first 150 s the temperature rises by 3.7 °C ✓
In the last 150 s it rises by only 3.1 °C, although the energy supplied in each interval is the same ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate $c$ using the readings at $t = 0$ and $t = 900\ \text{s}$.
markscheme: $E = VIt = 12.0 \times 3.50 \times 900$ J and $\Delta T = 40.3 - 20.0$ °C ✓
$c = \dfrac{E}{m\Delta T} = 4660\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: The accepted value of $c$ for water is $4180\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. Explain, with reference to your answer to (a), why the value in (b) is larger than the accepted value.
markscheme: The falling rate of rise shows that energy is lost to the surroundings, at a greater rate as the water gets hotter ✓
So less than $VIt$ goes into the water and $\Delta T$ is smaller than it would be with no losses; $c = \dfrac{VIt}{m\Delta T}$ is therefore too large ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate $c$ using only the first 150 s of heating.

parts.label: e
parts.question: Explain why using only the first 150 s reduces the effect of the energy losses.
markscheme: At the start the water is close to room temperature, so the rate of energy loss is small and almost all of $VIt$ goes into the water ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: The uncertainty in the value from (b) is about $\pm 170\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$ and in the value from (d) about $\pm 370\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. Discuss which value is the better estimate of $c$.
markscheme: (b) is more precise (smaller uncertainty), but its range, about 4490 to 4820, does not include 4180: it has a systematic error ✓

(d) has a larger uncertainty (small $\Delta T$), but its range, about 3890 to 4620, includes 4180: it is more accurate, so (d) is the better estimate (award for a conclusion consistent with the candidate's own values) ✓

stem:
A simple model treats a planet or moon as a black body with no atmosphere. It absorbs a fraction $(1 - \alpha)$ of the sunlight falling on it, where $\alpha$ is its albedo, and radiates energy from its whole surface. The temperature at which these balance is

$$T_\text{model} = \left(\frac{(1-\alpha)S}{4\sigma}\right)^{1/4}$$

where $S$ is the solar irradiance at the body. The table gives published data for five bodies. The graph shows the published mean temperature $T_\text{obs}$ against $T_\text{model}$; the point for Mars has not been plotted.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate $T_\text{model}$ for Mars.
markscheme: $T_\text{model} = 210\ \text{K}$ (accept 208 to 212 K) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Plot the point for Mars on the graph.
markscheme: Point at $T_\text{model} = 210\ \text{K}$, $T_\text{obs} = 208\ \text{K}$ (close to the dashed line), to within half a small square ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Identify the body whose temperature is furthest from the model. Explain why.
markscheme: Venus: about 510 K hotter than the model ✓

It has a very thick atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide: a strong greenhouse effect absorbs the infrared radiated by the surface and re-emits much of it back down, so the surface must be far hotter to radiate the absorbed energy away ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Use the graph to determine how much warmer the surface of the Earth is than the model predicts.
markscheme: The vertical distance of Earth's point above the dashed line: about 33 K (accept 23 to 43 K) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: On the Moon, the surface temperature at the equator ranges from 95 K at night to 390 K in the day. State one reason, other than the effect of the atmosphere, why the actual temperatures of planets and moons can differ from the model.
markscheme: Any one of: the temperature is not the same over the whole surface: it varies enormously between day and night (and from equator to poles), but the model assumes one uniform temperature / a single "mean temperature" depends on how it is averaged over such a wide range / emission depends on $T^4$, so a body with a wide range of temperatures radiates its energy at a lower mean temperature (the Moon lies below the line) / the surface is not a perfect black body ✓

stem: A student investigates how the pressure $p$ of a fixed mass of air at constant volume depends on its temperature $T$. A sealed flask of air is held in a water bath and connected by a short tube to a Bourdon pressure gauge. The bath is heated in steps, and at each step the student waits until the reading is steady.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show, using two rows of the table, that $p$ is not proportional to $T$.
markscheme: $\dfrac{p}{T}$ is 8.13 $\text{kPa}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ at 12.0 °C but 1.54 $\text{kPa}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ at 78.5 °C (or any two non-adjacent rows) ✓
The ratio is not constant, so $p$ is not proportional to $T$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Draw the line of best fit on the graph. Determine its gradient and its intercept on the $p$ axis.
markscheme: Gradient $= 0.34\ \text{kPa}\,{}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ (accept 0.33 to 0.36) ✓
Intercept $= 93.2\ \text{kPa}$ (accept 92.7 to 93.7) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Hence determine the temperature at which the pressure of the air would be zero, according to these data.
markscheme: At $p = 0$: $T = -\dfrac{\text{intercept}}{\text{gradient}}$ (extrapolating the line) ✓
$T = −272\ {}^{\circ}\text{C}$ (accept −280 to −262; allow ECF from (b)) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Draw the steepest and shallowest straight lines that pass through all the error bars. Use them to determine the absolute uncertainty in your answer to (c).
markscheme: Steepest and shallowest lines drawn through all the error bars ✓
Their temperatures at $p = 0$, found in the same way, are about −277 °C and −262 °C ✓
Uncertainty $= \dfrac{\text{difference}}{2} \approx 8\ {}^{\circ}\text{C}$ (allow values from the candidate's own lines) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The accepted value of absolute zero is $−273\ {}^{\circ}\text{C}$. Calculate the percentage difference between your answer to (c) and this value. Hence discuss whether your result is consistent with the accepted value.
markscheme: Percentage difference $= \dfrac{|−272 - (−273)|}{273} \times 100 \approx 0.4\,\%$ ✓
This is smaller than the percentage uncertainty from (d) (about 3 %), so the result is consistent with the accepted value (award for a conclusion consistent with the candidate's own uncertainty) ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: The flask is then placed in boiling water at 100 °C. Use your line of best fit to predict the reading of the pressure gauge.
markscheme: $p = 127\ \text{kPa}$ (accept 127 to 128) ✓

stem: A student investigates the internal resistance of a cell using the circuit shown. The student changes the resistance of the variable resistor $R$ and records the current $I$ and the potential difference $V$ across the terminals of the cell.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Identify the anomalous reading and suggest one possible cause of it.
markscheme: The reading at $I = 0.50\ \text{A}$, $V = 1.04\ \text{V}$ ✓
Any plausible cause, e.g. the voltmeter was misread / a poor connection / the reading was taken before the meters settled ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the emf $\varepsilon$ of the cell.
markscheme: Extends the line of best fit to $I = 0$: the emf is the intercept on the $V$ axis ✓
$\varepsilon = 1.52\ \text{V}$ (accept 1.51 to 1.54) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the internal resistance $r$ of the cell.
markscheme: From $V = \varepsilon - Ir$, the gradient of the graph is $-r$ ✓
$r = 0.75\ \Omega$ (accept 0.71 to 0.79) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in the reading of $V$ when $I = 0.80\ \text{A}$.

parts.label: e
parts.question: Suggest why the student should disconnect the circuit between readings.
markscheme: A current makes the cell warm up / makes the cell run down ✓
This would change $r$ (or $\varepsilon$) during the experiment, so the readings would not all describe the same cell ✓

stem: A student investigates how the period $T$ of a mass oscillating on a spring depends on the mass $m$. For each mass, the student times 10 oscillations with a stopwatch and divides by 10. The graph shows $T$ against $m$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Explain how the graph of $T$ against $m$ shows that $T$ is not proportional to $m$.
markscheme: The points lie on a clear curve: no straight line fits them ✓
The gradient decreases as $m$ increases (equal increases in $m$ give smaller increases in $T$) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: For a spring of negligible mass, $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{m}{k}}$, where $k$ is the spring constant. State the quantity that should be plotted against $m$ to give a straight line, and the gradient that line is expected to have.
markscheme: Gradient $= \dfrac{4\pi^2}{k}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: State the unit of the gradient of a graph of $T^2$ against $m$, in SI base units.

parts.label: d
parts.question: The student plots a graph of $T^2$ against $m$, shown below. Determine $k$.
markscheme: Gradient of the line of best fit $= 3.27\ \text{s}^2\,\text{kg}^{-1}$ ✓
$k = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{\text{gradient}} = 12.1\ \text{N m}^{-1}$ (accept 11.6 to 12.6) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The line of best fit on the graph of $T^2$ against $m$ does not pass through the origin. Explain what this suggests about the assumption that the spring has negligible mass.
markscheme: $T^2$ is not zero when $m = 0$: something else is oscillating, the spring itself, so its mass is not negligible ✓

The intercept on the $T^2$ axis is about 0.086 $\text{s}^2$; extended, the line would cross the $m$ axis at $m = -\dfrac{\text{intercept}}{\text{gradient}} \approx −0.026\ \text{kg}$: the spring behaves like an extra mass of about 0.026 kg added to $m$ ✓

stem:
A student investigates standing waves on a string. The string is attached to a vibration generator, passes over a pulley and supports a hanging mass $M = 0.200\ \text{kg}$, which keeps the tension $T$ in the string constant.

For different lengths $L$ of string between the vibration generator and the pulley, the student adjusts the frequency $f$ until the string vibrates in its first harmonic.

The speed of a wave on a string is $v = \sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$, where $\mu$ is the mass per unit length of the string.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Identify one variable that the student must keep constant so that the wave speed is the same for every length.
markscheme: The tension / the hanging mass (or: the same string, so the same $\mu$) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Show that the frequency of the first harmonic is $f = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$.
markscheme: There are nodes at both ends, so the first harmonic is half a wavelength: $\lambda = 2L$ ✓
$f = \dfrac{v}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the gradient of the graph of $f$ against $1/L$.
markscheme: Draws a line of best fit and uses two well-separated points on it ✓
Gradient $= 20.7\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ (accept 19.6 to 21.8) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Determine the mass per unit length $\mu$ of the string.

mistakes.feedback: The gradient is $\tfrac12\sqrt{T/\mu}$, not $\sqrt{T/\mu}$: check the factor of 4.

markscheme: Gradient $= \tfrac12\sqrt{\dfrac{T}{\mu}}$ with $T = Mg = 1.96\ \text{N}$, so $\mu = \dfrac{T}{4 \times \text{gradient}^2}$ ✓
$\mu = 0.0011\ \text{kg m}^{-1}$ (accept 0.0010 to 0.0013; allow ECF from (c)) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Calculate the percentage uncertainty in $1/L$ for $L = 0.500\ \text{m}$.
markscheme: The percentage uncertainty in $1/L$ equals that in $L$: $\dfrac{0.002}{0.500} \times 100 = 0.40\ \%$ ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: The student sets $L = 0.800\ \text{m}$ and increases the frequency until the string vibrates in its third harmonic. Use the graph to predict this frequency.

mistakes.feedback: That is the first harmonic. The third harmonic has three loops, so its frequency is three times larger.

markscheme: Reads $f_1 \approx 25.2\ \text{Hz}$ at $1/L = 1.25\ \text{m}^{-1}$ ✓
Third harmonic: $f_3 = 3f_1 = 75.6\ \text{Hz}$ (accept 73.4 to 77.9) ✓

stem:
Astronomers study a star in a binary system: the star moves in a circular orbit, so it moves alternately towards and away from Earth. They measure the wavelength $\lambda$ of a hydrogen line in its spectrum. In the laboratory this line has a wavelength of $656.28\ \text{nm}$.

The graph shows simulated observations on 18 nights: values generated from a model of the orbit, with the scatter a real spectrograph would give. Each wavelength has an uncertainty of $\pm 0.008\ \text{nm}$. The system as a whole is not moving towards or away from Earth.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Determine the orbital period of the star.
markscheme: Uses the times of two maxima (or minima) several cycles apart, for example about day 5 and day 28 (2 cycles) ✓
Period $= 11.6$ days (accept 10.4 to 12.7 days) ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the orbital speed of the star, in $\text{km s}^{-1}$.
markscheme: Largest shift from the laboratory wavelength, from the graph: $\Delta\lambda \approx 0.113\ \text{nm}$ ✓
$v = \dfrac{c\,\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}$ ✓
$v = 52\ \text{km s}^{-1}$ (accept 47 to 57; allow ECF from the shift read) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the percentage uncertainty in your answer to (b). The laboratory wavelength and $c$ are known precisely.
markscheme: The uncertainty in $\Delta\lambda$ is that of one wavelength reading, $0.008\ \text{nm}$ ✓
$\dfrac{0.008}{0.113} \times 100 \approx 7\,\%$ (allow ECF from (b)) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Predict the wavelength that would be observed on day 34.
markscheme: About half a period after the maximum near day 28, so near a minimum: $\lambda \approx 656.17\ \text{nm}$ (accept 656.164 to 656.196 nm) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Suggest one way in which the observations could be changed to determine the period more precisely.
markscheme: Any one of: observe for more cycles (a longer time) / observe more often, especially near the maxima and minima / fill the gaps in the record ✓

stem:
The table gives the semi-major axis $a$ (the mean orbital radius) and the orbital period $T$ of eight moons of Jupiter, taken from a NASA database. A student investigates whether the moons obey Kepler's third law, $T^2 \propto a^3$.

The graph shows $\lg(T/\text{day})$ against $\lg(a/\text{km})$. The point for Europa has not been plotted.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate the two missing values for Europa.

parts.label: b
parts.question: Suggest two reasons why a graph of $\lg T$ against $\lg a$ is used for these data, rather than a graph of $T$ against $a$.
markscheme: The values cover a very wide range ($a$ by a factor of about 90, $T$ by about 850): on ordinary axes most points would be crowded near the origin ✓
If $T = ka^n$, then $\lg T = n\lg a + \lg k$: a straight line whose gradient is the power $n$, which can be tested directly ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the gradient of the graph.
markscheme: Line of best fit; gradient from two well-separated points on the line ✓
Gradient $= 1.50$ (accept 1.47 to 1.53) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Deduce whether the data support Kepler's third law.
markscheme: $T^2 \propto a^3$ means $T \propto a^{3/2}$, so the gradient should be 1.5 ✓
The gradient found is equal to this, within the precision of reading the graph, so the data support the law ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: For a circular orbit, $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2a^3}{GM}$, where $M$ is the mass of Jupiter and $G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{N m}^2\,\text{kg}^{-2}$. Use a point on the line of best fit to determine $M$.
markscheme: Reads a point on the line, for example $\lg(a/\text{km}) = 6.000$ gives $\lg(T/\text{day}) = 0.810$ ✓
Converts to SI: $a = 1.0 \times 10^{9}\ \text{m}$ and $T = 558000\ \text{s}$ ✓
$M = \dfrac{4\pi^2a^3}{GT^2} = 1.9 \times 10^{27}\ \text{kg}$ (accept $1.8 \times 10^{27}$ to $2.1 \times 10^{27}\ \text{kg}$; allow ECF from the point read) ✓

parts.label: f
parts.question: The data come from a database, so the graph has no error bars. Suggest one reason why the gradient could still differ slightly from the value predicted by Kepler's third law.
markscheme: Any one of: the orbits are not perfect circles (Himalia's eccentricity is about 0.16) / the moons pull on each other / Jupiter is not a perfect sphere, so it does not act exactly as a point mass ✓

stem:
A student investigates the charges on oil drops. Drops are sprayed between two horizontal metal plates a distance $d = 6.00\ \text{mm}$ apart. The density of the oil is $875\ \text{kg m}^{-3}$.

The radius $r$ of each drop is found from its steady fall speed when the plates are not charged (you do not need this method). A potential difference is then applied, and adjusted until the drop stays still. The student records the voltmeter reading $V$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Show that the charge on a drop that stays still is $q = \dfrac{mgd}{V}$, where $m$ is the mass of the drop.
markscheme: The electric force balances the weight: $qE = mg$ with $E = \dfrac{V}{d}$, so $\dfrac{qV}{d} = mg$ and $q = \dfrac{mgd}{V}$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the missing values of $q$ for drops C and F.
markscheme: Mass from $m = \tfrac43\pi r^3\rho$; drop C: $q = 4.66 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ ✓
Drop F: $q = 6.30 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: The uncertainties in $V$, $d$ and the density are small compared with the uncertainty in $r$. Determine the percentage uncertainty in $q$ for drop A.

mistakes.feedback: The mass depends on r³: multiply the percentage uncertainty in r by 3.

markscheme: $\dfrac{\Delta r}{r} = \dfrac{0.005}{0.512}$, and $q \propto r^3$, so the percentage uncertainty is three times as large ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Deduce whether these data support the idea that charge comes in whole-number multiples of one smallest charge. Determine, from the data, the best value of that smallest charge.
markscheme: Every charge is close to a whole-number multiple (1, 2, 3, 4) of about $1.56 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ ✓
Each lies within its uncertainty (a few per cent, mostly from $r^3$) of that multiple, and no value lies halfway between multiples, so the data support quantisation ✓
Best value: total charge ÷ total number of charges (or the mean of $q/n$) $= 1.56 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ (accept 1.54 to 1.58) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The voltmeter is later found to read 3.0 % higher than the true p.d. Determine the corrected value of the smallest charge, and state the effect of this error on your conclusion in (d).
markscheme: The true p.d. is smaller, so every true charge is larger: $1.56 \times 1.030 = 1.61 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$ (allow ECF from (d)) ✓
Every charge is scaled by the same factor, so they are still whole-number multiples of one value: the conclusion about quantisation is unchanged ✓

stem:
A student investigates the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field. A magnet stands on a top-pan balance. A stiff, horizontal wire, held by a clamp, passes between the poles without touching the magnet. The length of wire in the field is $L = (5.0 \pm 0.2)\ \text{cm}$.

The balance is set to zero with no current in the wire. The student then measures the change in the balance reading, $\Delta m$, for different currents $I$.

parts.label: a
parts.question: State the direction of the magnetic force on the wire. Explain why the balance reading increases when there is a current in the wire.
markscheme: The force on the wire is upwards (from a hand rule, or the direction of $I\vec{L} \times \vec{B}$) ✓
By Newton's third law, the wire exerts an equal and opposite (downward) force on the magnet, so the reading increases ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Determine the gradient of the graph of $\Delta m$ against $I$.
markscheme: Draws a line of best fit and uses two well-separated points on it ✓
Gradient $= 0.325\ \text{g A}^{-1}$ (accept 0.312 to 0.340) ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Determine the magnetic flux density $B$ between the poles.
markscheme: Uses $F = \Delta m\, g$ with $\Delta m$ in kg, so $B = \dfrac{\text{gradient} \times 10^{-3} \times 9.8}{L}$ ✓
$B = 0.064\ \text{T}$ (accept 0.061 to 0.067; allow ECF from (b)) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Discuss whether the data support the hypothesis that the force on the wire is proportional to the current.
markscheme: The points lie on a straight line, within their error bars ✓
A straight line through all the error bars can pass through the origin, so the data support $F \propto I$ ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: The percentage uncertainty in the gradient is 4 %. Determine the absolute uncertainty in your value of $B$.

mistakes.feedback: That uses only the 4 % from the gradient. The length $L$ is uncertain too: add the percentage uncertainties.

markscheme: Percentage uncertainty in $L$ $= \dfrac{0.2}{5.0} \times 100 = 4\ \%$ ✓
Adds percentages: 4 % + 4 % = 8 %, so $\Delta B = 0.0051\ \text{T}$ (allow ECF from (c)) ✓

stem:
A student looks at a mercury vapour lamp through a handheld spectroscope. Bright lines of different colours are seen against a wavelength scale. The diagram shows part of the scale, with the three brightest lines in this part of the spectrum.

The second diagram shows some of the energy levels of a mercury atom.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Read the wavelengths of the three lines from the scale.
markscheme: Violet 405 nm, blue 436 nm, green 546 nm, each accepted within ±2.5 nm: any two correct ✓
All three correct ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: State the absolute uncertainty in each of your readings.
markscheme: $\pm 2.5\ \text{nm}$: half the smallest division (5 nm) of the scale ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Calculate the energy, in eV, of a photon of the green light.
markscheme: $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{546 \times 10^{-9}}$ J ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: A student suggests that all three lines are emitted by atoms falling from one and the same energy level. Deduce, using the energy levels, whether the suggestion is correct.
markscheme: Photon energies about 3.07, 2.85 and 2.28 eV (each uncertain by about ±0.02 eV) ✓
These match 7.73 − 4.67, 7.73 − 4.89 and 7.73 − 5.46 eV: all three are transitions from the 7.73 eV level, so the suggestion is correct (no other pair of levels gives these energies) ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Beyond the part of the scale shown, the mercury spectrum has two yellow lines, at 577.0 nm and 579.1 nm. Deduce whether readings from this scale could show that there are two lines.
markscheme: No: they are only 2.1 nm apart, less than the reading uncertainty of ±2.5 nm (and less than one 5 nm division), so they would be read as one line ✓

stem:
A student measures the count rate from a short-lived radioactive source with a Geiger–Müller tube and a counter. Every 30 s, starting at $t = 0$, the student records the number of counts $N$ in the 10 s interval that begins at time $t$.

With the source removed, the counter recorded 118 counts in 300 s. The corrected count rate $R$ is the mean count rate due to the source alone during each interval. One value of $R$ has been left for you to calculate.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Outline why the student measured the background count.
markscheme: The counter also detects background radiation, which must be subtracted to find the count rate due to the source alone ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the corrected count rate $R$ at $t = 210\ \text{s}$.

mistakes.feedback: Remember to subtract the background count first.

markscheme: Background counts in 10 s $= \dfrac{118}{30} = 3.9$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Use the graph to determine the half-life of the source.
markscheme: Draws a smooth curve of best fit and reads the time for $R$ to halve (from any starting value) ✓
Half-life $= 74\ \text{s}$ (accept 66 to 83) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: Explain why the percentage uncertainty in $R$ increases as $t$ increases.
markscheme: Decay is random, so the uncertainty in a count $N$ is about $\sqrt{N}$ ✓
The fractional uncertainty $\dfrac{\sqrt{N}}{N} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$ increases as $N$ falls ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: Suggest one change to the method that would reduce the uncertainty in the later values of $R$.
markscheme: Count for a longer interval (or repeat the experiment and average), so more counts are recorded ✓

stem:
The Krško nuclear power station in Slovenia has one reactor. Its thermal power is $1994\ \text{MW}$ and, in the years shown, its net electrical power output was $688\ \text{MW}$. The table gives the electrical energy $E$ it supplied in six years.

The load factor LF is the energy supplied as a percentage of the energy the station would supply at full power for the whole year. A year has 8760 hours (a leap year, such as 2020, has 8784).

One fission reaction in the reactor is

$${}^{235}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{1}_{0}\text{n} \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\text{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}\text{n}$$

Masses: $^{235}\text{U}$ 235.0439 u, neutron 1.0087 u, $^{141}\text{Ba}$ 140.9144 u, $^{92}\text{Kr}$ 91.9262 u.

parts.label: a
parts.question: Calculate the energy released in this fission reaction, in MeV.
markscheme: $E = 0.1859 \times 931.5 \approx 173\ \text{MeV}$ ✓

parts.label: b
parts.question: Calculate the load factor in 2018.
markscheme: $\dfrac{5490\ \text{GWh}}{0.688\ \text{GW} \times 8760\ \text{h}} \times 100 = 91.1\,\%$ ✓

parts.label: c
parts.question: Estimate the mass of $^{235}\text{U}$ that underwent fission in 2020. Assume that all the energy released in the reactor comes from the reaction above.
markscheme: Efficiency $= \dfrac{688}{1994} = 0.345$, so thermal energy $= \dfrac{6041 \times 3.6 \times 10^{12}}{0.345} = 6.3 \times 10^{16}\ \text{J}$ ✓
Number of fissions $= \dfrac{6.3 \times 10^{16}}{173 \times 1.60 \times 10^{-13}} = 2.3 \times 10^{27}$ ✓
Mass $= 2.3 \times 10^{27} \times 235.0439 \times 1.661 \times 10^{-27} \approx 890\ \text{kg}$ (accept 750 to 1000 kg; allow ECF from (a)) ✓

parts.label: d
parts.question: The reactor is shut down for refuelling about once every 18 months. Identify the years in the table in which it was not refuelled, and state the evidence.
markscheme: 2017 and 2020: the load factor is close to 100 % and the station was connected to the grid for 8708 and 8748 hours, compared with 88.1–91.8 % and 7849–8081 hours in the other years ✓

parts.label: e
parts.question: A gigawatt-year is the energy supplied by a power of 1 GW for one year. In 2020 the station supplied 0.69 gigawatt-years of electrical energy. A rule of thumb says that a reactor fissions about one tonne of $^{235}\text{U}$ for every gigawatt-year of electrical energy. Use your answer to (c) to deduce whether the 2020 data support this rule.
markscheme: Mass per gigawatt-year $= \dfrac{890\ \text{kg}}{0.69} \approx 1.3\ \text{t}$ (allow ECF from (c)) ✓

This is close to one tonne (the same order of magnitude), so the data roughly support the rule; accept a conclusion consistent with the candidate's value. (Not required: the estimate is a little larger because some energy comes from fissions of $^{239}\text{Pu}$ made in the fuel, which the calculation ignores.) ✓
